title: Adjectives of the third declension: πᾶς, πολύς, μέγας, ἀληθής

objectives.can: Parse πᾶς, πολύς, μέγας and adjectives in -ης and -ων, and match them to their nouns.

explanation.summary: Some of the commonest adjectives in the New Testament, πᾶς 'all, every', πολύς 'much, many' and μέγας 'great', do not decline like ἀγαθός, and neither do the adjectives of the type ἀληθής. They still do what every adjective does: they agree with their noun in case, number and gender.

sections.heading: πᾶς: one stem, two declensions
body: πᾶς has three forms in the nominative singular: πᾶς (masculine), πᾶσα (feminine) and πᾶν (neuter). The masculine and neuter follow the third declension on the stem παντ-: the genitive singular is παντός, the dative plural πᾶσιν. The feminine follows the first declension, with the stem πασ-: πᾶσα, πάσης, πάσῃ, πᾶσαν.
ἅπας is an emphatic form of πᾶς and is declined in the same way.

sections.heading: πᾶς with and without the article
body: The position of πᾶς with the article often changes its sense. Before a singular noun without the article it usually means 'every' or 'any': πᾶν δένδρον, 'every tree'. In the plural without the article it means 'all'. When πᾶς comes before the article and the noun, as in πᾶς ὁ ὄχλος, it usually means 'the whole' or 'all the', and so does the order article–πᾶς–noun, as in ὁ πᾶς νόμος, 'the whole law'. Before the article and a participle, πᾶς ὁ πιστεύων is 'everyone who believes'.
These are tendencies of the New Testament's usage, not rules without exceptions; the context decides.

sections.heading: πολύς and μέγας: two stems
body: These two adjectives are alike. In the masculine and neuter nominative and accusative singular they have a short stem: πολύς, πολύν, πολύ; μέγας, μέγαν, μέγα. In every other form they take a longer stem, πολλ- or μεγαλ-, with the ordinary endings of the first and second declension: πολλοί, πολλῶν, πολλή; μεγάλη, μεγάλου, μεγάλων.
So the nominative or accusative masculine singular and the neuter singular are the forms to watch. All the others are regular once you know the longer stem.

The analysed texts also file the comparative forms μείζων and πλείων under these headwords, because they are the comparative of the same adjectives. You will meet them in the next lesson, and the exercises on μέγας and πολύς may include them.

sections.heading: Adjectives in -ης and -ων
body: Adjectives such as ἀληθής 'true', ἀσθενής 'weak', πλήρης 'full', ὑγιής 'healthy' and μονογενής 'only, unique' have only two forms in the singular: one for masculine and feminine (ἀληθής) and one for the neuter (ἀληθές). In the plural these are ἀληθεῖς and ἀληθῆ. Their stem is of the same type as that of ἔθνος, so the genitive singular is ἀληθοῦς.
A smaller group in -ων, such as ἄφρων and σώφρων, has -ων for masculine and feminine, -ον for the neuter, and -ονος in the genitive.
The point to hold on to is that the same form serves both masculine and feminine, so the noun it belongs to, not the adjective, tells you the gender.

sections.heading: εἷς, οὐδείς and μηδείς
body: 'One' is εἷς in the masculine, μία in the feminine and ἕν in the neuter; the stem in the other cases is ἑν- (ἑνός, ἑνί, ἕνα) or μι- (μιᾶς, μιᾷ, μίαν). οὐδείς and μηδείς, 'no one, none', are built on the same forms: οὐδεμία, οὐδέν, οὐδενός. The analysed texts classify all three as adjectives, even though they often stand on their own as pronouns: 'no one', 'nothing'.

misunderstandings: The feminine of πᾶς is not third declension. πᾶσα, πάσης, πάσῃ and πᾶσαν follow the first declension.
ἀληθής is not a noun and not a masculine only: it is the form for masculine and feminine alike. In ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία it agrees with a feminine noun.
πᾶς with a singular noun and no article usually means 'every' or 'any', not 'all': πᾶν δένδρον is 'every tree'. With the article it more often means 'the whole'.

deeper.heading: Adjectives used alone
body: All of these adjectives can stand without a noun when the gender and number make clear what is meant: πάντες 'all people', πάντα 'all things', οὐδεὶς 'no one', οὐδέν 'nothing'. Greek readers supply the missing noun from the gender and number, and the reading habit is taught in a later lesson.

examples.analysis: μονογενοῦς is the genitive singular of μονογενής, and πλήρης follows it, 'full of grace'. μονογενοῦς has the genitive -οῦς of this class, the same pattern as ἔθνους. πλήρης is nominative singular, with the genitive χάριτος after it, 'full of grace'. Commentators discuss which noun it describes; because it is nominative, ὁ λόγος at the start of the verse is the usual choice.

check.prompt: ἀληθής ἐστιν ἡ μαρτυρία μου: why is ἀληθής the right form here?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is feminine nominative, like μαρτυρία, and the masculine and feminine are the same
It is the genitive of ἀλήθεια
It is neuter, agreeing with μου
check.explain: Adjectives in -ης use one form for masculine and feminine, so ἀληθής is a correct nominative singular feminine. It does not agree with μου, which is a pronoun in the genitive.

reading.why: Five verses with μονογενής, πλήρης, πάντες and οὐδείς, together with the third-declension nouns χάρις and πατήρ, in the prologue to John.
